_labels_order: signs[] order == model output order == labels.json
_credits: Reference: GISLR, Isolated Sign Language Recognition corpus (Deaf Professional Arts Network, Georgia Institute of Technology, Google), CC BY 4.0. Recorded by Deaf signers. Descriptions written for First Signs from the sources listed per sign; they are not from the dataset. Learn from Deaf teachers: these are memory aids.

signs.label: milk
signs.description: Hold your dominant hand in a loose C shape, then squeeze it closed into a fist twice, like milking a cow.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Fist-squeeze can look like YES (fist nodding at the wrist) at low frame rates; MILK opens and closes, YES bobs.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: drink
signs.description: Curve your dominant hand into a C as if holding a cup, and tip it toward your mouth.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Noun 'a drink' is often done with a small double movement. Alcohol variants use other handshapes.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: water
signs.description: Make a W with your dominant hand (three middle fingers up) and tap the index finger against your chin or lips twice.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint says lips, HandSpeak says chin; both are near the mouth.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: food
signs.description: Bunch the fingertips of your dominant hand together with your thumb and tap them against your lips, usually twice.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Same sign as EAT (HandSpeak). Lifeprint notes fluent signers often use just one tap. Lifeprint's page shows video only, so the handshape detail comes from HandSpeak.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: hungry
signs.description: Curve your dominant hand into a C, palm facing you, and slide it down the middle of your chest.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Same or nearly the same sign as WISH (both sources).

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: thirsty
signs.description: Run the tip of your dominant index finger down the front of your throat.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: A stronger movement with an intense face means CRAVE.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: apple
signs.description: Bend your dominant index finger into a hook, press its knuckle against your cheek near the mouth, and twist it back and forth.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint says cheek, HandSpeak says chin area. Some people use a fist instead of the hooked finger (Lifeprint calls that Signed English).

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: finish
signs.description: Hold both open hands up, fingers spread and palms facing you, then quickly twist them outward so the palms turn forward.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Used for 'all done'. One twist feels more final; a sharp one-handed version means 'stop it!'.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: please
signs.description: Place your flat dominant hand on the center of your chest and rub it in a circle a few times.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Two hands means ENJOY. Very close to HAPPY (flat hand brushing up the chest). Doing it with a fist instead is SORRY.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: thank you
signs.description: Start with the fingertips of your flat dominant hand near your lips, then move the hand forward and down toward the person you're thanking.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint notes it looks very similar to GOOD. HandSpeak's entry (https://www.handspeak.com/word/2186/) has no written description we could extract.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: sleep
signs.description: Hold your open dominant hand in front of your face, palm toward you, and draw it down toward your chin while the fingers close onto your thumb.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Hand ends in a bunched 'flattened O', not a fist. Similar to SLEEPY (fingers droop repeatedly) and to SAD (both open hands move down the face).

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: bed
signs.description: Tilt your head and rest your cheek against your flat palm (or both palms pressed together), like laying your head on a pillow.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint shows both one-hand and two-hand versions on either side of the head. Overlaps with the common 'sleeping' gesture.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: pajamas
signs.description: Unconfirmed: often a compound, SLEEP (open hand drawn down the face, closing) followed by CLOTHES (both open hands brushing down your chest).
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Not verified. Signing Savvy confirms PAJAMAS is an ASL compound, but its description is members-only. The SLEEP+CLOTHES parts come from Signing Time, which is not on our list. Lifeprint's page is empty and HandSpeak (https://www.handspeak.com/word/3673/) is video-only. A fingerspelled P-J is also used.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: This clip shows a P handshape followed by a J movement (PJs). We could not confirm this form on Lifeprint or HandSpeak, and the description (SLEEP + CLOTHES) is also unverified; check with a Deaf teacher.

signs.label: book
signs.description: Press both flat hands together, palms touching, then open them like a book while the little-finger edges stay together.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: A double movement is the noun BOOK; a single opening can mean OPEN-BOOK. Reversed (open to closed) means CLOSE-BOOK.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: night
signs.description: Hold your other arm flat in front of you, palm down. Rest your dominant wrist on its back with that hand bent down, like the sun setting.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Sliding along the arm means EVERY-NIGHT. TONIGHT = NOW + NIGHT. Mirror image of MORNING (hand rising).

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: kiss
signs.description: Touch the bunched fingertips of your dominant hand to your lower cheek, then to your upper cheek.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Sources disagree. HandSpeak's citation form is the cheek version above. Lifeprint's main version brings the fingertips of both bunched hands together in front of you with puckered lips (looks like MORE), and a one-hand version looks like HOME. Lifeprint says there are many variants.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: moon
signs.description: Curve your dominant index finger and thumb into a small C and tap it twice by the side of your forehead or eye.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint: same small-C handshape (crescent), with a version tapping around the eye. HandSpeak also lists a variant arcing outward from the forehead.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: shhh
signs.description: Hold your dominant index finger up against your lips while saying 'shh'.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Same as the everyday hearing gesture. Lifeprint uses it for 'be quiet', so it can be the first part of QUIET.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: wake
signs.description: Pinch each index finger and thumb together beside your eyes, then flick them open into L shapes, like eyes popping open.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint's WAKE-UP page shows it as opening eyes and glosses it as both 'wake up' and 'to be awake'. Similar to SURPRISE, which adds a surprised face.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: morning
signs.description: Hold your other arm flat across your body and put that hand by your dominant inner elbow. Raise your dominant forearm, palm up, like the sun rising.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: The movement is small. Mirror idea of NIGHT. A bigger movement means ALL-MORNING; a sideways sweep means EVERY-MORNING.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: bath
signs.description: Make two fists with thumbs up and rub them up and down on your chest, as if scrubbing yourself.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint warns it looks like ADDRESS/LIVE. BATH is a rubbing up-down-up movement, while ADDRESS is two quick upward thrusts.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: wet
signs.description: Hold both hands in front of you, palms up and fingers loose, then lower them slightly while closing the fingers onto the thumbs, twice.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint adds that many people start by touching a loose W to the chin (from WATER). Done gently it can mean SOFT, and a double movement can mean HUMID.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands. This clip begins with WATER (a W handshape at the chin) before WET; WET alone is the closing-hand part.

signs.label: dry
signs.description: Pull your dominant index finger across your chin or lips toward your dominant side, bending it into a hook as it moves.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Opposite direction to CEREAL, which also bends back and forth. UGLY is similar but done higher, under the nose, with a sour face.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: toothbrush
signs.description: Unconfirmed as a separate sign: move your dominant index finger side to side in front of your teeth, as if brushing them.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Not verified as TOOTHBRUSH. The description matches Lifeprint's BRUSH-TEETH text, but Lifeprint's toothbrush page is empty and HandSpeak's (https://www.handspeak.com/word/4739/) is video-only. Commonly the same sign as BRUSH-TEETH. Differs from TOOTH (a hooked finger tapping the teeth) mainly in the side-to-side movement.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: potty
signs.description: Make a T (thumb tucked between your index and middle fingers), palm facing out, and shake it side to side a couple of times.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: HandSpeak's POTTY entry says it is the TOILET sign, used for all ages. Lifeprint: the same sign means BATHROOM/TOILET, and some people twist instead of shaking.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: shower
signs.description: Hold your dominant hand above your head with the fingertips bunched, then flick the fingers open downward, like water spraying. Usually repeated.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint (animation only) says fluent signers use one or two movements. HandSpeak lists different signs for rain shower and baby/bridal shower.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: clean
signs.description: Hold your other hand palm up. Slide your flat dominant hand, palm down, across it from the heel out past the fingertips.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Same sign as NICE. A repeated movement means CLEAN-UP / cleaning.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: dirty
signs.description: Hold your dominant hand under your chin, palm down and fingers spread, and wiggle the fingers.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: DIRT/soil is a different sign (thumbs rubbing fingertips).

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: mom
signs.description: Spread the fingers of your open dominant hand and tap your thumb on your chin, often twice.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Variants: a single touch, wiggling fingers, or starting from a fist. Differs from DAD only in location (chin vs forehead). GRANDMA adds forward arcs.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: dad
signs.description: Spread the fingers of your open dominant hand and tap your thumb on your forehead, often twice.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: HandSpeak places it at the side of the forehead for citation. Wiggling the fingers is a common variant. Differs from MOM only by location; GRANDPA adds forward arcs.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: grandma
signs.description: Start as MOM (open hand, thumb on your chin), then move the hand forward away from your face in two small hops.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint says one big arc is also fine. A near-minimal pair with MOM and GRANDPA.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: grandpa
signs.description: Start as DAD (open hand, thumb on your forehead), then move the hand forward away from your head in two small hops.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: One big arc or a straight move forward is also used. A near-minimal pair with DAD and GRANDMA.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: brother
signs.description: Start with your dominant thumb (index finger out) at your forehead and bring it down onto your other index finger, both pointing forward side by side.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Both sources list a couple of handshape variants for the starting hand. SISTER is the same movement starting at the cheek/jaw.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: hello
signs.description: Touch your flat dominant hand to the side of your forehead, palm out, and move it away like a small salute, smiling.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Sources differ: HandSpeak gives the salute-from-forehead citation form; Lifeprint says a natural side-to-side wave is used. The salute can resemble DAD (thumb on forehead); a wave can resemble BYE.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: bye
signs.description: Hold your open dominant hand up, palm out, and wave by bending the fingers down and up at the knuckles a few times.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint: the natural wave; goodbye bends at the large knuckles or wrist, while hello sweeps side to side. HandSpeak's 'goodbye' entries are video-only.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: yes
signs.description: Make a fist and nod it up and down at the wrist, like a head nodding yes.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: HandSpeak: usually two nods. Fingerspelled Y-E-S is used for emphasis.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: no
signs.description: Hold your index and middle fingers together and snap them down onto your thumb, palm facing out, usually twice.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: One firm snap = a strong 'No!'. Gentle repeated snaps = a soft 'no, no' for a child. It comes from fingerspelled N-O.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: happy
signs.description: With your flat hand (or both hands), palm toward you, brush upward on your chest in small forward circles, smiling.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: One- and two-handed versions are both common. Close to PLEASE (one flat hand circling on the chest), which is a key confusable pair.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: sad
signs.description: Hold both open hands in front of your face, palms toward you, and draw them slowly down while making a sad face.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: A one-handed informal version exists (HandSpeak), which looks a lot like SLEEP without the closing fingers.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: cry
signs.description: Point your index fingers (one or both hands) just under your eyes and stroke them down your cheeks a few times, like tears.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Alternating hands, four fingers, or wiggling fingers mean crying hard or bawling.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: dog
signs.description: Hold your dominant hand up and snap your middle finger against your thumb twice.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Variants: pat your thigh then snap, or just pat your thigh twice (HandSpeak says the thigh pat is common with babies). The snap uses the middle finger, not the index finger.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: cat
signs.description: Pinch your dominant thumb and index finger together beside your nose and pull outward across your cheek twice, like stroking whiskers.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Handshape varies: F hand (most common), 8 hand, or G hand all mean CAT. Two-handed (both cheeks) is used for storytelling with young children.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: bird
signs.description: Hold your dominant index finger and thumb at the side of your mouth and open and close them twice, like a beak.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Look-alike: DUCK is the same idea but uses the index and middle fingers with the thumb (a bigger bill). BIRD can also mean 'chicken' in context.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: fish
signs.description: Hold your dominant hand flat with the palm facing sideways and wiggle it side to side as it moves forward, like a fish swimming.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Some signers add the other hand touching the wrist or elbow of the swimming hand; Lifeprint calls that version extra effort, but it is in use. Different from FISHING (casting a rod).

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: cow
signs.description: Put the thumb of your dominant Y hand (thumb and pinkie out) on your temple and twist the hand up and down, like a horn.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Two-handed (both temples) is the version often used when signing to young children; one hand is used in everyday conversation.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: horse
signs.description: Put the thumb of your dominant hand on your temple with your index and middle fingers up together, then bend those fingers down twice, like a horse's ear.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Two-handed (both sides of the head) is used when signing to children. Using all four fingers instead of two means DONKEY. Look-alike: COW is also at the temple but uses a Y hand that twists.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: car
signs.description: Hold two fists in front of you and move them up and down alternately, like turning a steering wheel.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Fingerspelling C-A-R is just as common (Lifeprint recommends it). Very similar to DRIVE; HandSpeak warns learners to keep the hands as fists (S hands), not thumbs-up fists. An older version taps two C hands together.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: outside
signs.description: Put your dominant fingertips into your other hand's loose C shape, then pull them up and out while closing your fingers together.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Common one-handed version: open hand closing as it moves up and out, done twice, which both sources give for 'outside / outdoors'. One single movement means GO-OUT.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). A one-handed OUTSIDE is also common in everyday ASL.

signs.label: jump
signs.description: Stand the tips of your dominant index and middle fingers on your other palm like legs, then lift them up and land them back down.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Repeat the hop for 'jumping'. Look-alikes: DANCE (the same two-finger legs swinging side to side over the palm) and RIDE (bent fingers sitting on the other hand moving forward).

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: balloon
signs.description: Start with both curved hands together in front of your mouth, then move them apart in a round shape, as if a balloon is inflating as you blow.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Lifeprint describes it as miming blowing up a balloon; the noun is smaller and quicker, the verb 'blow up a balloon' larger and slower.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: airplane
signs.description: Make an 'I love you' hand (thumb, index and pinkie out), palm down, and move it forward a short way twice.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Angle the palm down so it is not just the I-LOVE-YOU sign. A single long forward sweep means FLY. HandSpeak also shows a version with the index and middle fingers crossed.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: owie
signs.description: Point both index fingers toward each other and jab them together twice, near the spot that hurts.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: OWIE is signed with the general HURT/PAIN sign; Lifeprint's pain page uses the word 'owie' for it. A twisting version (fingers twist in opposite directions) is also common, and HURT can be fingerspelled quickly near the sore spot. Use a pained face.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: sick
signs.description: Touch your dominant bent middle finger to your forehead and your other bent middle finger to your stomach at the same time.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: HandSpeak shows a common one-handed version, forehead only.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: mad
signs.description: Hold your dominant open hand in front of your face and bend the fingers into a claw once, with a scrunched, angry face.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Don't touch your face. A double movement with a milder face means 'grumpy'. ANGRY is a related sign: both claw hands pulled up from the stomach. The facial expression is part of the sign.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: like
signs.description: Start with your dominant thumb and middle finger open near your chest, then pull the hand forward while pinching them together.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Uses the middle finger, not the index; HandSpeak warns not to confuse the handshape with the one in WHITE. LIKE never means 'similar' (that's SAME).

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: wait
signs.description: Hold both open hands up to one side, palms toward you, and wiggle your fingers.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Wiggling longer, with a bored face, means 'wait a long time'.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: up
signs.description: Point your dominant index finger upward and move it up a little.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: A double movement can mean 'upstairs'. DOWN is the same idea pointing down.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: open
signs.description: Hold both flat hands side by side, palms down, then swing them apart so the palms turn up, like opening double doors.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Verified from HandSpeak's text; Lifeprint's page is pictures only and says opening something specific (a door, window, jar) is often mimed instead. Look-alike: BOOK starts with palms pressed together and opens like a book.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
video.note: Signed one-handed here (the signer is holding a phone). In everyday ASL, use both hands.

signs.label: hot
signs.description: Hold a bent, claw-like hand in front of your mouth, then quickly twist and throw it down and away, as if removing something hot.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: A faster, stronger movement means hotter.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: look
signs.description: Point your dominant index and middle fingers out from under your eyes, then turn them forward toward what you are looking at.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Verified from HandSpeak's text; Lifeprint's LOOK page is pictures only. The sign points toward the thing being looked at, so its direction changes.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0

signs.label: where
signs.description: Hold up your dominant index finger, palm out, and shake it side to side a few times from the wrist, with your eyebrows down.
signs.credit: Reference: GISLR (D-PAN / Georgia Tech / Google), CC BY 4.0
signs.note: Furrowed eyebrows are part of WH-questions. Use a plain index finger. An older version shaking two palm-up hands now mostly means WHAT.

video.credit: PopSign ASL v1.0 (Georgia Tech / DPAN), Deaf signer gtsignstudy4a.8037, CC BY 4.0
